name: Middle Mongol
confidence_why: Nugteren 2011 states outright that Middle Mongol accent is not known and that the Middle Mongol sources give no support for initial accent (repeated in Nugteren 2020), and the only positive claims are weaker and point in opposite directions: Saitô 1996 finds free accent with a general tendency toward the final syllable in Western Middle Mongol, Atwood 2023's pronunciation note puts stress on the first syllable, and Poppe 1954, Grønbech & Krueger 1955 and Poppe 1965 describe Classical Written or modern Mongolian rather than Middle Mongol.
catalog_citation: Nugteren, Hans. 2011. Mongolic Phonology and the Qinghai-Gansu Languages. Utrecht: LOT (LOT 289; Leiden University dissertation). Open access:https://www.lotpublications.nl/Documents/289_fulltext.pdf
catalog_locator: p. 39 (section 1.5, discussion of a North-South division; text between page footers 38 and 39) and p. 63, section 2.4.3 'Accent placement' (between footers 62 and 63); also p. 60, section 2.4 and p. 67, section 2.5.4.
catalog_quote: p. 39: "This seems to be supported by other features, such as initial accent in the North and final accent in the South, and preservation of the distinction between attributive and enumerative numerals in the North, lost in the South. However, the impression of a North-South division is not confirmed by Middle Mongol, which may side with either region, or may be indecisive (e.g. Middle Mongol accent is not known)." p. 63 (2.4.3. Accent placement): "In the Shirongol languages the accent normally falls on the last syllable. ... Moghol has final accent as well. The QG languages show vowel reductions in unaccented syllables, and the complete loss of such syllables. ... Given that Dagur and central Mongolic normally place the accent on the first syllable, one may conjecture that this represents the original situation, and that the QG languages and Moghol shifted the accent under Turkic and Iranian influence. However, the Middle Mongol sources do not provide support for such an assumption. Notably the reduction of unaccented syllables is not in evidence." p. 60 (2.4. Undecided matters in Common Mongolic): "In three matters specifically the QG languages provide us with additional information, without leading to a definitive solution: ... and placement of the accent (which was probably non-distinctive)."
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (extracted text of the open-access LOT 289 PDF, 562 pages, page numbers checked by form-feed count). Both quoted passages are there verbatim at the stated locators: printed p. 39 (pdf page 39, section 1.5.1.4 'Lexical features' discussion of a North-South division), lines 1600-1603: "However, the impression of a North-South division is not confirmed by Middle Mongol, which may side with either region, or may be indecisive (e.g. Middle Mongol accent is not known)."; printed p. 63, section '2.4.3. Accent placement', lines 2811-2816: "Given that Dagur and central Mongolic normally place the accent on the first syllable, one may conjecture that this represents the original situation, and…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The most authoritative accessible source states explicitly that the position of the Middle Mongol accent is not known: the written sources show no reduction of unaccented syllables, so they neither confirm nor refute the conjecture (based on Dagur and central Mongolic) that accent was originally on the first syllable. Secondary/reading-pronunciation sources for Written (Classical) Mongolian put the stress on the first syllable (Poppe 1954 §15, p. 9: 'always falling upon the first syllable regardless of vocalic length'; Grønbech & Krueger 1955 §3: non-phonemic, read on the first syllable), and Atwood's 2023 translator's note says stress on Middle Mongolian names 'is generally on the first syllable'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned for Middle Mongol in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Middle Mongol. Nugteren notes (p. 76) that the restriction of *o/*ö to first syllables 'may be an indication for initial accent, at least in the period when this distribution of the vowels was established' (i.e. pre-Middle-Mongol), and that modern Dagur/central Mongolic have initial accent while Shirongol/Moghol have final accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Extinct corpus language attested only in scripts (Uighur-Mongolian, 'Phags-pa, Chinese and Arabic transcriptions); no direct evidence of accent placement. The statement concerns word-level accent; Nugteren adds (p. 60) that Common Mongolic accent placement is an undecided matter and 'probably non-distinctive'.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement (Nugteren 2011) is about Middle Mongol proper (13th-14th c. corpus language, Glottolog midd1351). The positive first-syllable statements found (Poppe 1954 §15; Grønbech & Krueger 1955 §3) describe Written/Classical Mongolian reading pronunciation, which Glottolog files under midd1351 via Janhunen's 'Written Mongol' chapter but which is a different (literary, Uighur-script) variety; Glottolog's midd1351 page lists no alternative names or dialects. Atwood 2023 is a translator's pronunciation guide for Middle Mongolian names, not a description.

For the purposes of reading a text in the classical language, however, the accent may be placed on the first syllable throughout.' — Classical Written Mongolian.

tone.quote: (4)表記上のゆれをもって現れる語があり、それは母音の弱化および消失が起こっていたことを示していると考えられる。その母音の弱化および消失は、西部中期モンゴル語は「ストレスが主として語末に置かれる自由アクセントの言語」であったことを示している。 / [author's English summary:] (4) Some graphic fluctuations indicate that vowel reduction and deletion were occurring in the language. These phenomena show that West Middle Mongolian was a free stress accent language where the stress tended to be placed on the last syllable of a word.
tone.locator: KAKEN project page KAKENHI-PROJECT-06610465: Japanese text under 研究概要, item 2(4) on the /ja/ page; the author's English version under 'Research Abstract'
tone.translation: (4) Some words appear with fluctuating spellings, which is taken to show that vowel weakening and loss were taking place. That vowel weakening and loss shows that West Middle Mongolian was 'a free-accent language in which stress was placed mainly on the word-final syllable'.
tone.summary: No tone discussed; free (non-fixed) stress accent, predominantly word-final (West Middle Mongol).
